'''Michael A. Zasloff''' (born July 2, 1946) is an American [[physician]], [[medical research]]er, and entrepreneur.  Zasloff is primarily known for his work on antimicrobial peptides.

==Early life==
Michael Alan Zasloff was born to a [[American Jews|Jewish]] family, the son a dentist and an artist. Growing up on [[West Side (Manhattan)|Manhattan's West Side]], he studied at the [[Bronx High School of Science]].<ref name=frogs>{{cite news|last1=Okie|first1=Susan|title=A Man and His Frogs|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/1988/02/16/a-man-and-his-frogs/8ae0f57d-5c40-4c52-be7f-47105159d5cb|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=February 16, 1988}}</ref>

==Education==
Zasloff did his undergraduate work at [[Columbia University]]<ref name=people/> and earned his M.D. and Ph.D. from the [[New York University School of Medicine]].<ref name=macrochem/>

He did his residency training in pediatrics at the [[Boston Children's Hospital]] and a research fellowship at [[Johns Hopkins University]].<ref name=atlantic/> In 1975 he joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) as a postdoc.<ref name=atlantic/>

==Professional career==
Zasloff stayed at the NIH after he finished his postdoc, and in 1981 he was made the Chief of the Human Genetics Branch of the National Institutes of Child Health and Human Development.<ref name=macrochem>{{cite news|title=Press release: MacroChem Corporation Announces Michael Zasloff, M.D., Ph.D. Joins Company's Scientific Advisory Board|url=https://www.biospace.com/macrochem-corporation-announces-b-michael-zasloff-m-d-ph-d-b-joins-company-s-scientific-advisory-board|work=MacroChem via BioSpace|date=October 17, 2007}}</ref> In 1986 he discovered [[magainin]]s, a family of antimicrobial peptides in the skin of the African clawed frog.<ref name=atlantic/><ref>{{cite news|last1=Altman|first1=Lawrence K.|title=Staying Ahead of Microbes: New Progress|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/08/04/science/the-doctor-s-world-staying-ahead-of-microbes-new-progress.html?pagewanted=all|work=The New York Times|date=4 August 1987}}</ref><ref name=Conlon>{{cite journal|last1=Conlon|first1=JM|last2=Mechkarska|first2=M|last3=King|first3=JD|title=Host-defense peptides in skin secretions of African clawed frogs (Xenopodinae, Pipidae).|journal=General and Comparative Endocrinology|date=1 May 2012|volume=176|issue=3|pages=513–8|doi=10.1016/j.ygcen.2011.10.010|pmid=22036891}}</ref><ref name=people>{{cite web |title=The Case of the Frog That Healed Leads Dr. Michael Zasloff to a Medical Leap Ahead |work= [[People Magazine]]|last=Brower|first= Montgomery|location= [[New York City|New York]], [[New York (state)|New York]]|date= 17 August 1987 | url= http://people.com/archive/the-case-of-the-frog-that-healed-leads-dr-michael-zasloff-to-a-medical-leap-ahead-vol-28-no-7/}}</ref>

Magainin Pharmaceuticals, Inc. was founded in the late 1980s to commercialize the peptides. Zasloff left the NIH at about the same and went to University of Pennsylvania, in part because the NIH policies made it difficult for him to participate in the company.<ref name=atlantic/>  Magainin eventually went public and its name was changed to Genaera.  The company attempted to develop [[squalamine]], [[trodusquemine]], and pexiganan (a version of a magainin), but the company closed in 2009 without having brought any products to market.<ref>{{cite news|last1=George|first1=John|title=Biotech Genaera shutting down: Never brought drug to market |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/philadelphia/stories/2009/04/27/daily31.html|work=Philadelphia Business Journal|date=April 29, 2009}}</ref>

At Penn, working with Fred Kaplan, Zasloff continued research he had begun at the NIH on the cause and treatment of [[fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva]].<ref name=atlantic>{{cite news|last1=Maeder|first1=Thomas|title=A Few Hundred People Turned To Bone|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1998/02/a-few-hundred-people-turned-to-bone/304887/|work=The Atlantic|date=February 1998}}</ref>

Zasloff left Penn in 1992 and joined Magainin full time.<ref>{{cite web|title=Zasloff bio|url=https://gufaculty360.georgetown.edu/s/faculty-profile?netid=maz5|publisher=Georgetown University|accessdate=16 January 2018|language=en}}</ref>   He was with the company until its lead product, pexiganan, was rejected by the FDA in 1999 for lack of efficacy compared with the standard of care for diabetic foot ulcers, and he went to Georgetown University's medical school, where he was appointed Dean for Research and Translational Science.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Moore|first1=A|title=The big and small of drug discovery. Biotech versus pharma: advantages and drawbacks in drug development.|journal=EMBO Reports|date=February 2003|volume=4|issue=2|pages=114–7|doi=10.1038/sj.embor.embor748|pmid=12612596|pmc=1315844}}</ref>  In 2011 Zasloff found that squalamine had antiviral activity.<ref>{{cite news|title=Press release: GUMC Discovery Chosen for Time's Top 100 Scientific Findings|url=https://gumc.georgetown.edu/news/discovery-chosen-for-time|work=Georgetown|date=May 2, 2013|language=en}}</ref>

In 2013 Zasloff co-founded a company called Formula XO that sold haircare products.<ref>{{cite web|title=Formula XO Company Profile: Valuation & Investors|url=https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/88335-28|publisher=PitchBook|accessdate=16 January 2018|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Corsano|first1=Erica|title=Russo's Illumai creates beauty without beastly chemicals|work=Boston Herald|date=October 16, 2014|page=28}}</ref>

He later co-founded a company called Enterin, that intended to develop a derivative of squalamine called kenterin as a treatment for Parkinson's disease; the company received its first round of venture funding in 2017.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Taylor|first1=Phil|title=Backers put $12.7M behind Enterin's Parkinson's disease approach|url=https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/backers-put-12-7m-behind-enterin-s-parkinson-s-disease-approach|work=FierceBiotech|date=July 17, 2017|language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Zasloff is married to Dr. Barbara Zasloff, a clinical psychologist (whom he met when they were undergraduates at Columbia University), and they have three daughters.<ref name=frogs/>
